strengths: Significance: The paper targets an important practical gap—evaluating text-to-image systems on genuinely long, detail-intensive prompts—and provides a comparatively large benchmark of 4,116 prompts averaging 284.89 tokens.

Originality: DETAILMASTER combines four useful dimensions—character attributes, character locations, scene attributes, and entity relationships—at substantially greater prompt length and annotation density than the cited benchmarks. The structured spatial annotations and full/mini benchmark variants are valuable additions.

Empirical scope is strong: 12 general-purpose and long-prompt-oriented models are evaluated, including modern open and proprietary systems. The resulting tables expose meaningful differences across model generations and task dimensions.

The authors make several worthwhile robustness efforts, including auditing benchmark annotations, repeating evaluation with InternVL3-9B, reporting Kendall rank correlations, testing evaluator randomness, and documenting compute requirements.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. Pipeline diagrams, per-dimension results, configuration details, failure cases, and an explicit limitations section make the contribution easy to understand.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central automated evaluator is not validated against human judgments on generated images. The human study checks whether benchmark annotations match source images and prompts, but does not measure the precision, recall, or agreement of the Qwen-based scoring pipeline—the mechanism producing every headline model score.

Changing the evaluator from Qwen to InternVL produces very large absolute score shifts, sometimes exceeding 20 percentage points. Preserved model rankings are useful but do not establish that the reported accuracy values are calibrated or even correct; rank agreement alone is insufficient validation for a benchmark metric.

Several central conclusions are causal or mechanistic without controlled evidence. Claims that long-prompt training matters more than context capacity, that encoders flatten grammatical structure, and that diffusion models exhibit attribute leakage are inferred from comparisons among models that differ simultaneously in backbone, training data, resolution, inference procedure, and architecture. The paper itself acknowledges that the proposed mechanisms lack direct validation.

The prompt-length analysis is substantially confounded: longer prompts likely contain more entities, attributes, and relationships and therefore create harder images independently of sequence length. The paper provides binned plots but no correlation coefficients, uncertainty estimates, hypothesis tests, or regression controlling for constraint count, entity count, source dataset, or visual complexity.

Generation uncertainty is not characterized. The manuscript does not clearly report multiple generated samples or generation seeds per prompt, confidence intervals, or significance tests. A single stochastic realization can materially affect comparisons, while Appendix J tests only evaluator randomness rather than image-generation randomness.

Benchmark validity is limited by its synthetic construction: prompts are expansions of existing image captions rather than naturally occurring user requests, and the audit finds nontrivial source-image mismatches, including only 88.58% relationship alignment and 91% lighting alignment. This weakens claims about authentic real-world long-prompt behavior and may encode Qwen-specific linguistic patterns.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript. Appendix E paraphrases much of the prompting procedure instead of supplying complete templates and few-shot examples; sampling and decoding settings for the curation/evaluation models and generation seeds are insufficiently specified; and proprietary API endpoints with default settings can drift. The paper promises release of data and code but provides no verifiable artifact here.

The human audit reports only two annotators and averaged scores, without inter-annotator agreement, adjudication procedures, uncertainty, annotator recruitment details, or a sufficiently clear sampling protocol. Thus, statements such as “near-perfect” quality are stronger than the presented evidence supports.

Limitations and ethics treatment is too narrow. It discusses metric coverage and compute cost but not demographic/geographic bias, privacy or identifiable people inherited from image datasets, annotation labor, dataset licensing and redistribution, or misuse of detailed image generation. The small NSFW-detector experiment on outputs from four models does not address these broader concerns.

strengths: Significance/originality: DETAILMASTER is a useful, comparatively large benchmark targeting an important weakness of text-to-image systems. Its 4,116 prompts average 284.89 tokens, cover 12 models, and decompose adherence into character attributes, locations, scene attributes, and entity relationships.

The evaluation is broad: it includes general-purpose and long-prompt-specialized systems, reports results for a resource-efficient 800-prompt subset, and provides conditioned attribute results that help separate character omission from attribute-binding errors.

The construction and evaluation pipelines are described in substantial detail, including model configurations, compute requirements, localization procedures, annotation counts, and case studies. The authors also examine evaluator choice and evaluator randomness.
Presentation is generally organized and understandable, and the paper honestly acknowledges the computational cost and extensibility of its metrics.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central automated evaluator is not validated against human judgments on generated images. The human study evaluates benchmark annotations against source images and prompts, not whether Qwen's yes/no decisions on model outputs are correct. Re-evaluation with InternVL establishes rank correlation between two automated evaluators, but correlated rankings do not establish either evaluator's validity; absolute scores change dramatically.

The dual-model presence detector requires agreement between Qwen and YOLOE, so detector false negatives propagate into attribute, location, and relationship scores. No human-labeled generated-image set, detector precision/recall analysis, or metric-level agreement with humans is provided. This is a major construct-validity gap for the paper's principal results.

The claimed effect of prompt length is confounded with prompt complexity: longer bins likely contain more entities, attributes, and relationships. Figure 3 provides binned trends without controlled prompt variants, effect sizes, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. It therefore does not support a causal conclusion that length itself causes degradation.

Claims that long-prompt training matters more than context capacity, and that iterative decomposition drives improvement, come from comparisons among models differing simultaneously in backbone, training data, resolution, architecture, and inference procedure. These cross-model observations cannot isolate the proposed causal factors.

Benchmark prompts are machine-expanded descriptions of existing images, rather than independently authored user requests. Human inspection itself finds only 88.58% image alignment for entity relationships and roughly 91% for person and lighting attributes. Incorporating hallucinated annotations into the prompt may preserve internal prompt-label consistency, but it does not preserve the claimed fidelity to authentic real-world requirements and can introduce unnatural or contradictory targets.

The data-quality study is underspecified: it reports only two annotators, gives no agreement statistics or adjudication process, and ambiguously states that 50 samples per task produce 400 samples. The study is also too small to characterize rare errors across 4,116 prompts and tens of thousands of annotations.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the promised release. Full prompt templates and few-shot examples are not included, image-generation sampling variability is not evaluated, confidence intervals are absent, and proprietary API versions can change. There is also no contamination analysis even though prompts derive from COCO, Flickr30k, and DOCCI images that may overlap model training data.

The limitations and ethics discussion is inadequate. It omits source-data licensing and privacy, annotator recruitment/compensation, demographic and cultural bias, contamination, evaluator bias across visual styles, and misuse considerations. The limitations section mainly mentions missing aesthetic metrics and computational cost rather than the central validity threats.

Presentation has several inconsistencies and overclaims: GPT-4o versus GPT Image-1 naming differs between the setup and tables; 'Entity Relationships' is sometimes called 'Spatial Attributes'; scene scores are nearly saturated without investigating evaluator leniency; and hypotheses about grammar flattening and attribute leakage are explicitly untested yet are framed prominently as explanatory findings.

strengths: Significance: DETAILMASTER addresses a useful and underexplored evaluation setting—detail-intensive prompts averaging 284.89 tokens—with 4,116 prompts, 37,165 character attributes, 6,910 locations, and 18,526 relationships.

Originality: The combination of character-level attributes, structured locations, scene properties, and entity relationships provides broader diagnostic coverage than the cited long-prompt benchmarks.

Soundness: Evaluation across 12 general-purpose and long-prompt-optimized models is extensive. The comparisons expose plausible capability gaps and a consistent ranking of recent systems over older baselines.

Robustness and reproducibility: The paper reports inference configurations, computational costs, evaluator-seed experiments, an alternative InternVL3 evaluator, a resource-efficient 800-prompt subset, and intends to release data, construction code, and evaluation tools.
Presentation: The pipeline is clearly organized, with informative diagrams, detailed appendices, human checks of benchmark annotations, and candid discussion of computational limitations.
weaknesses: The central automated evaluator is insufficiently validated against human judgments on generated images. Human evaluation checks source annotations, not whether Qwen2.5-VL's per-attribute decisions are correct. Agreement of aggregate model rankings with InternVL does not establish item-level validity because both evaluators may share biases.

Absolute scores are highly evaluator-dependent: switching to InternVL raises many results by roughly 15–30 percentage points. Thus claims such as state-of-the-art systems achieving only about 50% accuracy are not robust, even if relative rankings are.

The prompt-length analysis is confounded by content difficulty. Naturally longer prompts likely contain more characters, attributes, and relationships; binning by length without controlling these factors or constructing matched prompt truncations does not establish that length itself causes degradation.

Claims that long-prompt training matters more than context capacity are drawn from comparisons among methods that also differ in backbones, training data, architecture, resolution, and inference procedures. These results are suggestive rather than causal.

Generation stochasticity is not adequately assessed. Appendix J varies evaluator randomness but does not report multiple generated images or seeds per prompt, leaving uncertainty about the stability of model comparisons—especially for proprietary APIs.

Data-quality validation uses only two annotators, reports no inter-annotator agreement or qualifications, and finds only 88.58% source-image alignment for relationships. Ethics and limitations coverage should also address dataset licensing, privacy, demographic/geographic representation, and potential biases inherited from source datasets and MLLM annotation.

strengths: Significance/originality: DETAILMASTER targets an important and comparatively underexplored setting—faithful generation from dense, structured prompts—and contributes 4,116 prompts averaging 284.89 tokens with annotations for character attributes, locations, scene attributes, and relationships.

Soundness: The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering 19 models across classical diffusion, long-prompt-specific, LLM/MLLM-encoder, unified, and proprietary systems. The 2×2 study separating context length from training-prompt length is a useful experimental design.

Evaluation robustness: The paper reports alternative evaluators, Kendall correlations of 0.879–1.0, repeated stochastic evaluations, a human audit of 400 task samples, and a smaller 800-prompt benchmark. These checks materially strengthen the resource.

Presentation: The construction and evaluation pipelines are clearly illustrated, extensive implementation and computational details are supplied, and the fine-grained metrics reveal useful failure patterns that aggregate alignment scores would obscure.
weaknesses: Soundness: The automatic evaluator—the foundation of nearly every reported result—is not validated directly against human judgments on generated images. The human study audits prompt/annotation construction instead. Agreement between Qwen and InternVL rankings cannot establish correctness because both evaluators may share systematic errors; indeed, their absolute scores differ dramatically, sometimes by over 30 points.

Soundness: Character presence requires agreement between an MLLM and YOLOE, after which absent detections automatically suppress attribute and relationship credit. This can conflate detector recall with generation quality and create cascading errors. No human-estimated precision/recall or sensitivity analysis is reported for this gate.

Soundness: The causal claims exceed the evidence. Cross-model comparisons confound encoder quality with architecture, scale, resolution, and training data, so they do not verify that weak encoders specifically fail to preserve syntax. Likewise, decreasing accuracy across length bins does not isolate prompt length from the correlated number and difficulty of constraints; matched prompts with controlled truncation or expansion are absent.

Soundness/reproducibility: The ablation models are trained on two million pairs sampled from the same source datasets—DOCCI and Localized Narratives—from which DETAILMASTER is constructed, but the manuscript does not establish image-level or semantic train/test disjointness. Domain overlap or direct leakage could materially inflate the claimed benefit of long-prompt training.

Statistical evidence: The paper reports point estimates without confidence intervals or tests for model differences, length trends, or the ablation effects. It also does not clearly report multiple image-generation seeds per prompt. Consequently, small differences and the claimed interaction between context capacity and training length are not established statistically.

Reproducibility/presentation: Although the paper promises to open-source data and code, no concrete repository or artifact is provided in the manuscript. Exact generation seeds and sufficiently precise versioning for changing proprietary APIs are also missing; heterogeneous resolutions further complicate fair reproduction.

Limitations/ethics: The impact statement claims that no societal consequences require discussion. This is inadequate for a benchmark built from real-image datasets and used to assess generative models: dataset licenses, privacy, demographic and cultural coverage, representational bias, objectionable prompt content, and the limitations of automated safety checking warrant explicit treatment.

strengths: Significance: Long-prompt compositional generation is a useful evaluation target, and the benchmark is substantial: 4,116 prompts, structured annotations, four diagnostic dimensions, and results for 19 models spanning several architectural families.

Originality: The combination of unusually long prompts (284.89 tokens on average), character-level attributes and locations, scene properties, and entity relationships offers finer diagnostics than a single holistic alignment score, although the underlying decomposition-and-VQA approach is not fundamentally new.

Soundness-positive: The authors include several worthwhile checks, including annotation inspection by two experts, an alternative InternVL evaluator, a smaller Qwen evaluator, evaluator-randomness experiments, and a 2x2 token-limit/training-prompt ablation.

Reproducibility and presentation: The manuscript describes the construction and evaluation pipelines, inference settings, compute requirements, model variants, prompts, and a mini benchmark. The main tables and figures make the broad empirical trends understandable.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive concern: The central automated metric is never validated against human judgments on generated images. The human study evaluates whether constructed annotations match source images and prompts, not whether Qwen2.5-VL's yes/no decisions correctly score model outputs. Agreement in model rankings between two MLLMs—whose absolute scores differ dramatically—demonstrates correlation, not metric validity. Consequently, the reported accuracies and rankings cannot yet support the paper's central benchmark claims.

The character-presence gate requires agreement between an MLLM and YOLOE, after which all attributes and relationships involving an undetected character fail or are skipped. No detector precision/recall analysis is supplied on generated images, where distortions and unusual styles are common. Metric scores may therefore conflate generation failures with detector failures and systematically favor photorealistic or easily detected outputs.

The claimed effect of prompt length is heavily confounded. Longer prompts also contain more entities, relations, rare attributes, and difficult scenes; the paper bins raw length and plots accuracy without controlling for constraint count or difficulty, reporting uncertainty, or performing statistical tests. These results establish an association but not that length itself causes degradation.

The 2x2 ablation does not cleanly isolate context capacity from long-prompt training. The short condition uses LLM-compressed captions of at most 30 tokens, whereas the long condition changes both length and information density; under a 77-token limit, long prompts are additionally sensitive to constraint ordering and truncation. Only one training run is reported, with no confidence intervals, and essential optimization details such as learning rate, batch size, training steps, and random seeds are absent. Claims that long-prompt training matters more and that the two factors are synergistic are therefore stronger than the evidence.

Benchmark representativeness is insufficiently justified. Prompts are selected for more than four main characters and repeatedly expanded by Qwen models from image captions. They are not sampled from professional user workflows, despite being motivated as proxies for such workflows. Some annotations have only 88.58% source-image agreement for relationships and 91% for lighting; incorporating hallucinated properties into the final prompt makes scoring internally consistent but weakens the claim that the benchmark is grounded in realistic images and logic.

The evaluation appears to use a single stochastic image per prompt and does not report generation-seed replication or uncertainty. Repeating only the evaluator cannot establish stability with respect to image-generation variance. Comparisons also mix 512×512 and 1024×1024 outputs and mutable proprietary APIs/defaults, creating additional fairness and reproducibility concerns.

Presentation and interpretation: The manuscript is readable and extensive, but repeatedly turns correlational evidence into mechanistic conclusions—for example, attributing failures to encoder syntactic parsing, diffusion-model attribute leakage, or real-world positional priors. These hypotheses are plausible but are not isolated experimentally. The paper also lacks confidence intervals, effect-size analyses, and annotator agreement statistics.

Originality is moderate rather than high: decomposing prompts into atomic constraints and using an MLLM/VQA evaluator closely follows existing benchmark methodology. The main novelty is increased prompt length and annotation density, whose value depends critically on the currently missing evaluator validation.

Ethics and limitations are treated inadequately. The impact statement says no consequences require discussion, despite reliance on web-derived images, detailed descriptions of people, proprietary services, and MLLMs with potential demographic and stylistic biases. Licensing, privacy, annotator protocol, representation bias, and the benchmark's susceptibility to evaluator gaming are not substantively addressed. Overall, the work has useful ingredients, but the unvalidated central metric and confounded analyses are important evidential deficiencies that prevent acceptance.

strengths: Significance: DETAILMASTER targets an important weakness of current text-to-image systems that is underrepresented in existing benchmarks. Its 4,116 prompts are substantially longer than prior benchmarks (284.89 tokens on average), and the decomposition into character attributes, locations, scene attributes, and relationships offers useful diagnostic granularity.

Empirical breadth: The evaluation covers 19 systems across classical diffusion, long-prompt-specific, LLM/MLLM-encoder, unified, and proprietary model families. The resulting tables expose meaningful performance differences and persistent weaknesses even in frontier models.

The authors make several valuable robustness and accessibility efforts: a 400-item human audit of benchmark annotations, evaluation with alternative 3B and InternVL evaluators, evaluator-randomness experiments, an 800-prompt mini benchmark, and reporting of inference configurations and computational costs.

Presentation and originality: The construction and evaluation pipelines are clearly illustrated, the appendix is extensive, and the benchmark's combination of unusually dense prompts with character-specific structured constraints is a useful, moderately original contribution.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed evaluator prompts, model inference settings, resource estimates, and a stated commitment to release data and code.
weaknesses: Soundness—most decisively, the generated-image evaluator is not validated against human judgments. The human study checks annotation-to-source-image and annotation-to-prompt consistency, not whether Qwen2.5-VL's yes/no decisions on generated images are correct. Agreement in model rankings between automated evaluators does not establish validity because both may share systematic errors; indeed, switching to InternVL changes many absolute scores by 20–35 points.

The requirement that both an MLLM and YOLOE detect a character can turn detector failures into generation failures. This then cascades into attribute and relationship scores. No human audit quantifies this error, so the reported accuracies cannot be cleanly interpreted as prompt adherence.

The prompt-length analysis is observational and substantially confounded: longer prompts likely contain more entities, attributes, relationships, and intrinsically difficult scenes. Binned curves without matched prompts, multivariate controls, confidence intervals, or statistical tests do not support the causal claim that length itself causes degradation or attribute leakage.

Several mechanistic conclusions overreach the evidence. Comparisons among models that simultaneously differ in encoder, generator, scale, architecture, and training data cannot establish that weak encoders fail to preserve syntax or that diffusion models specifically cause attribute leakage.

The 2×2 ablation is insufficiently specified and analyzed. The paper does not clearly state train/evaluation splits despite deriving both the benchmark and the claimed two-million-pair training set from DOCCI and Localized Narratives, creating a serious possible leakage concern. Optimization details, training duration, generation seeds, and repeated-run uncertainty are absent. The small differences receive no significance analysis, and merely obtaining the best result when both factors are enabled does not demonstrate a statistical interaction or 'synergy.'

Cross-model comparison has uncontrolled variation: SD1.5-family outputs use 512×512 while most others use 1024×1024; proprietary systems use changing API endpoints and defaults; and the manuscript does not report repeated image-generation seeds or uncertainty over stochastic generations. Fine-grained detection accuracy can depend on resolution and sampling.

The benchmark is presented as representative of professional instructions, but prompts are machine-expanded reconstructions of existing images rather than collected professional requests. Human checks find only 88.58% source alignment for relationships and about 91% for person attributes and lighting, and no inter-annotator agreement is reported. This weakens claims of realism and near-perfect quality.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive appendix: the visible manuscript provides no usable repository/data link, some model and training details are missing, and proprietary API results will be difficult to reproduce as endpoints evolve.

Ethics and limitations are treated inadequately. The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not discuss licensing and release conditions for derived datasets, privacy or demographic bias in person attributes, evaluator bias beyond model-family affinity, or risks associated with detailed prompts and generated people. A dedicated limitations discussion should distinguish benchmark validity limitations from limitations of current T2I systems.
